<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par141 />{{GHGmargin-letter|141|i}}
Of (''b''): naturally this does not apply to the examples, in which {{GHGheb|text=הָיָה}}, in the sense of ''to become, to fare, to exist'', still retains its full force as a verb, and where accordingly the sentence is verbal, and not a noun-clause; especially when the predicate precedes the subject. On the other hand, such examples as {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=1|verse=2}} ''and the earth was'' ({{GHGheb|text=הָֽיְתָה}}) ''waste and emptiness'', can scarcely be regarded as properly verbal clauses; {{GHGheb|text=הָֽיְתָה}} is used here really only for the purpose of referring to past time a statement which, as the description of a state, might also appear in the form of a pure noun-clause; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=3|verse=1}}. This is especially true of the somewhat numerous instances in which {{GHGheb|text=הָיָה}} occurs as a connecting word between the subject and the participial predicate; e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=1|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=1|verse=14}} (immediately afterwards a pure noun-clause). The imperfect of {{GHGheb|text=הָיָה}} announces what is future in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=14|verse=33}}, &c.; cf. {{GHGpar|116|r}}. However, especially in the latter case, {{GHGheb|text=הָיָה}} is not wholly without verbal force, but comes very near to being a mere copula, and this use is more frequent in the later books<ref>According to Albrecht, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZAW.|Zeitschrift für die alttestamentliche Wissenschaft, ed. by B. Stade, Giessen, 1881 ff., and since 1907 by K. Marti.}}}} viii. 252, especially in Deuteronomy and in the Priestly Code.</ref> than in the earlier.

{{GHGmargin-letter|141|k}}
Rem. On the employment of {{GHGheb|text=יֵשׁ|translate=existence}}, and {{GHGheb|text=אַ֫יִן|translate=non-existence}}, which were originally substantives (on their tendency to be used as verbs, equivalent to ''est'', and ''non est'', cf. {{GHGpar|100|o}}, and the ''Negative Sentences'', § 152) as a connecting link between a pronominal subject and a participial predicate (especially in conditional and interrogative sentences, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=42}}, 49, 43:4, &c.), see above, {{GHGpar|116|q}}, and the various kinds of subordinate clauses mentioned in §§ 150, 159.

{{GHGmargin-letter|141|l}}
'''4.''' The natural ''arrangement'' of words in the noun-clause, as describing a state, is ''subject—predicate''; the principal stress falls on the former since it is the object of the description. Very frequently, however (and not merely in poetry, where greater freedom is naturally allowed in the arrangement of words), the reverse order is found, i.e. ''predicate—subject''. The latter order ''must'' be used when special emphasis is laid on the predicate,<ref>For the same reason specifications of place (e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=4|verse=7}}) or other adverbial qualifications may stand at the beginning of the sentence.</ref> or when it consists of an interrogative word; thus with a substantival predicate, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=3|verse=19}} {{GHGheb|text=עָפָר אַתָּה|translate=dust thou art}}; 4:9, 12:13 (''my sister'', not my wife); 20:2, 12, 29:14, Is 6<sup>3 ''b''</sup>, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=5|verse=24}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=6|verse=12|hidebook=1}}; with an adjectival predicate, e.g. Is 6<sup>3 ''a''</sup>, 28:21, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=10|verse=6}}; with a participle, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=30|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=32|verse=12|hidebook=1}}; with an interrogative pronoun, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=65}};<ref>The only exceptions, according to Albrecht (see the Rem. above), are {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=16|verse=7}}, 8.</ref> with an adverbial interrogative, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=4|verse=9}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|141|m}}
Rem. On the above cf. the exhaustive investigations of C. Albrecht, ‘''Die Wortstellung im hebr. Nominalsatze'',’ {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZAW.|Zeitschrift für die alttestamentliche Wissenschaft, ed. by B. Stade, Giessen, 1881 ff., and since 1907 by K. Marti.}}}} vii. 218 ff. and viii. 249 ff.; with a complete list of the exceptions to the order ''subject—predicate'', p. 254 ff. The predicate ''must'' precede for the reasons stated (an ''adjectival predicate'' is particularly emphatic when it has the force of a comparative, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=4|verse=13}}; the predicate expressed by means of a preposition precedes most frequently when it serves to convey the ideas of ''having, possessing'', e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=18|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=29|verse=16|hidebook=1}}, &c.; cf. also 26:20, 31:16, 43).

{{GHGmargin-letter|141|n}}
